tema: Money Idioms — The Language of the Wallet

vocabulario.traduccion: costar un ojo de la cara

a penny saved is a penny earned

cast_dialogue.linea: Money has its own poetry, heroes. Idioms turn wallets into stories — learn them and you'll understand what numbers hide.
My new lens cost an arm and a leg, but I didn't want to put all my eggs in one cheap basket.
When I opened the restaurant, money was tight. We were in the red for six months!
I save a little for a rainy day every month. I don't want to live from hand to mouth.
Money doesn't grow on trees, mis héroes. A penny saved is a penny earned — but sometimes, splash out on cake!

banco_oraciones.oracion: The renovation cost an arm and a leg.
Now the business is in the black.
He saved some money for a rainy day.
Last month she splashed out on a new oven.
He didn't throw money down the drain.
They aren't living from hand to mouth anymore.
We didn't break the bank on the holiday.
Did the car cost an arm and a leg?
Is the company in the red or in the black?
Do you save for a rainy day?
Did he go bankrupt? No, he didn't.
Is money tight this month? Yes, it is.
Did you splash out? Yes, I did.

banner_diagnostico.opcion_a: The renovation cost an arm and a leg.
banner_diagnostico.opcion_b: The renovation cost an arm and a hand.

inicio.definicion_pragmatica: Money idioms are fixed expressions: 'cost an arm and a leg' (very expensive), 'in the red/black' (losing/making money), 'tighten your belt' (spend less), 'splash out on' (spend freely). They don't translate word by word — learn them as complete pictures.

ejercicios.pregunta: The renovation cost ___. It was incredibly expensive.
After six bad months, the restaurant is finally ___.
I save a little ___ — you never know what will happen.

ejercicios.afirmacion: 'To tighten your belt' means to spend more money.
'To live from hand to mouth' means to live with just enough money to survive.

ejercicios.texto: He didn't want to put all his ___ in one basket.
Money ___ grow on trees, you know!

ejercicios.respuesta: Don't throw money down the drain.

ejercicios.texto_con_error: The renovation cost an arm and a hand.
ejercicios.respuesta: The renovation cost an arm and a leg.
The car cost an arm and a leg.
The company was in the red.

ejercicios.pregunta: Describe your relationship with money using three idioms.
ejercicios.respuesta: I save for a rainy day. I never throw money down the drain. Sometimes I splash out on books.

guion: Sofía: Kenji, how did the restaurant survive its first year?
Kenji: With difficulty! Money was tight, and the renovation cost an arm and a leg.
Sofía: So you were in the red?
Kenji: For six months. But I didn't throw money down the drain — I saved for a rainy day.
Kenji: Now we're in the black! Last month I even splashed out on a new oven.
Kenji: Yes: don't put all your eggs in one basket.

comprension.pregunta: How long was the restaurant in the red?
What did Kenji splash out on?

reading.texto: When Kenji opened his restaurant, money was tight and he had to tighten his belt. The renovation cost an arm and a leg, and at first the business was in the red. But Kenji didn't throw money down the drain: he saved pennies for a rainy day. Now the restaurant is in the black, and last month he splashed out on a new oven. His advice? Don't put all your eggs in one basket.

preguntas.afirmacion: Kenji advises putting all your eggs in one basket.
